canonical_concept.beeja: ॐ itself is the mahā-bīja (great seed syllable) — the source of all other bīja mantras.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Om is classified as a praṇava (primordial sound) and an avyaya (indeclinable). It is not declined like ordinary nouns. Pāṇini treats it as a sacred syllable (maṅgala-vācaka). The written form ॐ is a ligature of the three letters A, U, M with the anusvāra (nasal resonance) and the bindu (point of silence above).
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Om is the sonic representation of Brahman — the absolute reality expressed as vibration. It is used as a prefix to all mantras, prayers, and sacred texts. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad teaches that Om encompasses all of time (past, present, future) and all states of consciousness. Meditation on Om leads to the direct experience of Brahman.
canonical_concept.dhatu: अव् (Av) — To protect, to pervade. Some traditions derive Om from the root av (to protect) or from the three letters A-U-M representing creation, preservation, dissolution.
canonical_concept.nirukta: Yāska: Om is the name of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this. The three letters represent the three states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep) and the three worlds.
canonical_concept.tattva: Praṇava-Tattva — the principle of the primordial sound. Om is the sonic form of Brahman — the vibration from which the universe emerges and into which it dissolves.

claims.value: In Vedic cosmology: Om is the sound of the universe — the cosmic vibration (nāda-brahman) from which all creation emerges. claims.value: Meditation on Om (Om-japa, Om-dhyāna) is the primary practice for stilling the mind. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad maps the four parts of Om (A, U, M, silence) onto the four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turīya). The practice of Om-kāra-dhyāna (meditation on Om) leads through all four states to the recognition of Ātman = Brahman.

claims.value: The written symbol ॐ represents: A (waking state/creation), U (dreaming state/preservation), M (deep sleep/dissolution), the curve above (māyā/illusion), the dot (turīya/liberation), the silence after (Brahman). The three curves represent the three states of consciousness. The dot represents the fourth state (turīya) — pure awareness.

It suggests that when we realize all of life is one, we stop hurting ourselves by hurting others, and what we do to others will one day be done to us. This principle, also known as "Do unto others as you would have others do unto you," promotes treating others with love, compassion, and kindness [1]. The yugas are also associated with changes in the color of Lord Narayana and the stability of dharma, with each yuga having a shorter span of life and increased distress.

The streets, quadrangles, and highways were sprinkled with water perfumed with sandal and aloe, and adorned with flowers, unbroken rice, fruits, and lights [1]. Ideal cities were also beautified with stems of bananas, young arecas, and festoons prepared with leaves of various trees [1]. Additionally, the cities had a strong emphasis on cleanliness, with streets and quadrangles being regularly cleaned and perfumed [2]. Overall, the key features of an ideal city in ancient Indian texts included cleanliness, beauty, and a strong sense of community, with an emphasis on decoration, perfume, and adornment [1], [2].

functional_meaning.summary: Om is the sonic representation of Brahman — the absolute reality expressed as vibration. It is used as a prefix to all mantras, prayers, and sacred texts. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad teaches that Om encompasses all of time (past, present, future) and all states of consciousness. Meditation on Om leads to the direct experience of Brahman.
